stem: A relation R on set A = {1, 2, 3} is defined as R = {(1,1), (2,2), (3,3)}. Which property does R satisfy?

per_option_rationale.rationale: R is reflexive, but it also satisfies symmetric and transitive, so identifying only one property understates it.
R is symmetric (trivially, since all pairs are of the form (a,a)), but it also has reflexive and transitive properties.
R is transitive (vacuously and by diagonal pairs), but it also satisfies reflexive and symmetric properties.

R = identity relation on A. It is reflexive (each (a,a) is present), symmetric ((a,b) in R implies (b,a) in R, trivially true since only equal pairs exist), and transitive (if (a,b) and (b,c) are in R then a=b=c so (a,c) = (a,a) is in R). Hence R is an equivalence relation.

explanation: The identity relation {(1,1),(2,2),(3,3)} on any set A is the simplest equivalence relation. It is reflexive because every element is related to itself. It is symmetric because (a,b) in R means a=b so (b,a)=(b,b) is also in R. It is transitive because (a,b) and (b,c) both in R force a=b=c, so (a,c)=(a,a) is in R.

explanation_sections.punchline: The identity relation {(a,a) : a in A} satisfies all three properties and is the canonical equivalence relation.
explanation_sections.approach: State the three definitions, test each against the relation, and confirm all hold. For the identity relation every test is trivial.
explanation_sections.lesson: Reflexive: (a,a) in R for all a. Symmetric: (a,b) in R => (b,a) in R. Transitive: (a,b) and (b,c) in R => (a,c) in R. All three together = equivalence.
explanation_sections.timing: 35 s. Do not stop at reflexive; check all three before choosing.
